tldr: The authors identified that Diffusion Policy collapses to a single action modality (mode collapse) even when trained on balanced and symmetric datasets. To fix this without changing inference or policy architecture, they proposed an approach that optimally matches actions and noise within each training mini-batch using the Hungarian algorithm, recovering diverse action modalities.
hero_caption: Comparison of noise space structuring in the Push-T task. In the vanilla method, noise samples corresponding to the two action modalities are mixed together. In the proposed method (Immiscible), Hungarian matching separates the noise space by modality, forming regions that preserve action diversity.
overview:
Diffusion Policy applies diffusion models to action generation and has been expected to possess "multimodality"—the ability to generate diverse action trajectories from different initial noise samples. However, the authors discovered that even in tasks like Push-T with perfectly symmetric clockwise and counterclockwise pushing, and even when training mini-batches are kept strictly symmetric, the trained model almost always collapses to a single action modality (mode collapse).

Analyzing why this happens, they found that robot action spaces are low-dimensional and dense compared to images. Random (independent) pairing of actions and Gaussian noise causes diffusion paths in the reverse process to heavily intersect and mix (miscibility). As a result, the denoiser fails to distinguish between modalities and produces an averaged response. Minor optimization asymmetries then cause only one mode to survive. Inspired by Immiscible Diffusion in image generation, the authors proposed "Immiscible Diffusion Policy," which matches action chunks and noise samples with minimal distance within each mini-batch strictly during training.

Evaluating the approach across five simulated tasks and two real-world humanoid robot tasks demonstrated that it powerfully restores lost action modalities without altering the model architecture or inference sampler. Across three two-modality tasks, the non-dominant-modality proportion increased by $6.0\times$ to $14.6\times$, and the method successfully recovered action modalities that had completely vanished under the vanilla policy in four-modality tasks.
contributions: Experimentally and theoretically demonstrated that standard Diffusion Policy collapses to a single action modality even when datasets are fully balanced and within-batch symmetry is guaranteed.
Uncovered the mechanism behind mode collapse: crossing and mixing of diffusion paths (miscibility) and reduced noise sensitivity in low-dimensional action spaces.
Proposed Immiscible Diffusion Policy, a label-free training-time plug-in that pairs actions and noise via Hungarian matching without altering policy architecture or the inference pipeline.

Demonstrated across seven simulation and real-world humanoid tasks (covering state, RGB, and point-cloud observations) that the method dramatically recovers lost action diversity while maintaining strong task performance.

sections.heading: Why Does Diffusion Policy Forget Diverse Actions?
sections.summary: Although Diffusion Policy was expected to model multimodal action distributions, it often collapses to a single action even on symmetric data. Preserving multiple strategies (multimodality) is vital for robustness against environment changes, and this work proposes a label-free plug-in method to solve this issue.
sections.details:
In many robot manipulation scenarios, multiple valid action strategies exist for the same situation. For example, in Push-T when the T-block starts facing opposite to the target, pushing it clockwise or counterclockwise are both valid solutions. Intuitively, different initial Gaussian noise samples should map to these alternative action trajectories. In practice, however, across all 10 independent seeds, the policy collapsed to only one rotational direction. Enforcing exact within-batch bilateral symmetry during training failed to prevent this collapse.

Losing action multimodality is critical when deployed in changing environments with distribution shifts, such as obstacles. Because the model has forgotten the alternative behaviors available during training, it cannot adapt to avoid failures. Prior work attempted to handle this using modality annotations, specialized latent spaces, or modified inference procedures, but these approaches are hard to apply in continuous spaces with an unknown number of modes.

To address this, the authors developed "Immiscible Diffusion Policy," which organizes action-noise pairings only during training without changing the model architecture or inference sampler. By coupling noise and actions using Hungarian matching (an optimal assignment algorithm), it prevents diffusion paths from crossing and preserves diverse modalities.

sections.heading: Related Work: Multimodal Action Modeling and Data-Noise Pairing
sections.summary: Compared to existing approaches for robot action diversity (latent-variable models or action discretization), this work tackles an unaddressed mode collapse inherent to standard diffusion models. It adapts noise assignment techniques from image generation to robot control, focusing on preserving action diversity rather than generation efficiency.
sections.details:
### II-A Action Multimodality in Robot Learning
Many formulations have been explored to capture multimodal actions in robot learning. For instance, latent-variable models like ACT and Play-LMP learn latent plans, but require specialized representation learning. Implicit Behavioral Cloning (energy-based models) suffers from heavy iterative optimization at inference, and models like Behavior Transformer rely on explicit action discretization. Diffusion Policy emerged as a powerful paradigm directly expressing multimodality in continuous spaces. This paper identifies a severe issue inherent to the standard model—modalities disappear during training even with balanced data—and prevents it without structural modifications.

### II-B Data-Noise Assignment in Diffusion Models
In diffusion and flow-based models, structuring the mapping between data and noise (such as optimal transport in Flow Matching) has primarily served to straighten trajectories and accelerate training or sampling. Immiscible Diffusion in computer vision also reduces path crossing to speed up training. However, robot action spaces are far lower-dimensional and denser than image spaces, with clusters lying close together, making mode collapse from path crossing exceptionally severe. This work differs fundamentally by introducing data-noise coupling not for generation speed, but to preserve action multimodality.

sections.heading: Why Does Mode Collapse Occur? Pinpointing Denoiser Desensitization
sections.summary: Comparing an analytically derived ideal denoiser with trained models reveals that collapse is not a limitation of the diffusion process itself, but happens because the learner becomes insensitive to noise variations. Independent noise pairing in low-dimensional spaces leads to averaged outputs, losing modality bifurcations.
sections.details:
### III-A Modality Collapse in Diffusion Policy
In Push-T, even when each batch contained equal numbers of demonstrations for both rotational directions, rollouts across all 10 random seeds collapsed almost entirely to a single mode (the dominant mode occupied an average of 97.6% per seed). Furthermore, the preferred direction varied across seeds, indicating that the collapse stems from training dynamics rather than geometric bias.

### III-B Why Action-Modality Collapse Happens
To investigate the cause, the authors built an analytical "ideal denoiser" computed directly from training demonstrations based on the formulation by Karras et al. The ideal denoiser generated both modes in a balanced manner even with finite sampling steps, producing 174 distinct action chunks from 256 initial noise samples. In contrast, the trained vanilla denoiser collapsed to an average of just 2.6 distinct actions (and only 1 action for some seeds).

Why does this happen? Standard training pairs action chunks with Gaussian noise independently at random. Because robot actions form dense clusters in low dimensions, adding noise causes different modal distributions to overlap over wide noise regions. In these overlapping regions, the optimal solution minimizing MSE (mean squared error) loss is simply the average of the modes.

Ideally, the denoiser should bifurcate into two modes as the noise level decreases. But with independent noise pairing, no modal cues exist in the noise space, so this bifurcating response becomes extremely weak when learning from finite data. Measuring the output variation along the axis connecting both mode centers (the modality-response range), the ideal denoiser scored 4.29, while the vanilla model achieved only 0.24 (5.6%). As the denoiser becomes insensitive to noise variations, slight asymmetries from stochastic optimization pull all noise inputs toward a single surviving mode.

sections.heading: Proposed Method: Label-Free Noise Assignment via Hungarian Matching
sections.summary: By establishing a one-to-one mapping between action chunks and noise samples within each mini-batch using the Hungarian method to minimize distance, distinct modal regions are carved out in noise space. It is a lightweight training-only technique requiring zero changes to model architecture or inference.
sections.details:
### IV-A Immiscible Diffusion Policy
The core idea of Immiscible Diffusion Policy is to couple action chunks and noise samples to suppress diffusion path crossings, ensuring each action modality originates from a distinct region in Gaussian noise space.

Let $B$ be the mini-batch size. For normalized action chunks $\mathbf{a}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_a}$, Gaussian noise vectors $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_j$ are sampled independently from a noise pool of the same size. After an initial warmup phase during training, the policy computes the Euclidean distance matrix between coordinate-standardized action vectors in the batch and noise vectors. It then finds the permutation $\pi^*$ minimizing the sum of squared distances via the Hungarian algorithm:

$$\pi^* = \arg\min_{\pi \in \mathcal{S}_B} \sum_{i=1}^B \left\| \frac{\mathbf{a}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_B}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}_B} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\pi(i)} \right\|^2$$

Using the matched noise, the standard forward diffusion process is carried out, and the noise prediction network is trained with MSE loss. Crucially, because noise vectors are merely permuted within each batch, the marginal noise distribution remains standard Gaussian. No additional loss functions, extra gradient computations, or inference modifications are needed.

### IV-B How Noise Assignment Preserves Action Multimodality
Although this assignment uses no explicit modality labels, it maps natural cluster structures in action space directly into noise space. Similar action chunks are matched with spatially close noise vectors, naturally grouping the noise space by modality.

Evaluating the modality-response range, the vanilla model reached only 0.24 (5.6% of ideal), while the proposed method maintained 1.93 (about 45% of ideal). Near the midpoint, its response magnitude was roughly $8.3\times$ higher than vanilla. This allows the denoiser to retain mode-specific trajectories even at overlapping noise levels, preventing mode collapse.

captions.F2: Noise space distributions in Push-T. In Vanilla, noise samples for Mode 1 (yellow) and Mode 2 (blue) are completely mixed. In Immiscible, they are clearly separated along the modality axis, allowing initial noise to retain action modality information.

sections.heading: Experiments: Restoring Lost Modalities Across Simulation and Real Humanoids
sections.summary: Evaluated across five simulation tasks and two real-world humanoid tasks, the proposed method maintained task performance while substantially boosting the non-dominant modality proportion and recovering action modes that had completely dropped to 0% under Vanilla.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
In simulation, the authors evaluated Push-T, plus two dual-modality tasks (Stack Blocks, Place Bread) and two four-modality tasks (Place Shoe, Rotate QR Code) from the dual-arm RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark, totaling five tasks. For real-world hardware, they used a Unitree G1 humanoid on two tasks (Fruit-to-Plate placing a banana, and Can-to-Bin dropping a can into a bin), both executable with either arm. Observations spanned low-dimensional states, RGB images, and 3D point clouds (using 3D Diffusion Policy). Metrics included Total Variation (TV) distance from a uniform modal distribution and task success rate.

### V-B Experiment Results
Vanilla Diffusion Policy suffered severe mode collapse despite perfectly balanced training data: in dual-modality tasks, the dominant mode took over 95% of rollouts (Push-T: 97.60%, Stack Blocks: 96.67%, Place Bread: 95.56%). In four-modality tasks, the fourth modality collapsed completely to 0.0% generation in both Place Shoe and Rotate QR Code. On the real humanoid, all rollouts collapsed to a single arm.

In contrast, Immiscible Diffusion Policy dramatically improved diversity. The proportion of non-dominant modes in dual-modality tasks surged from 2.40% to 35.00% on Push-T, 3.33% to 20.00% on Stack Blocks, and 4.44% to 33.33% on Place Bread—an average increase of $8.68\times$. On the real humanoid, arm usage balanced cleanly to a 1:1 distribution. Furthermore, in four-modality tasks, Mode 4 was restored to 16.0% and 11.1% respectively, maintaining near-balanced representation across all modalities.

Task performance remained strong: in simulated dual-modality tasks, Push-T coverage went from 95.16% to 95.39%, and Stack Blocks maintained a 96.67% success rate, showing virtually no degradation.

### V-C Analysis and Ablation Studies
Investigating the minor drop in overall success rate on four-modality tasks revealed that performance on the original modes favored by Vanilla remained comparable. The slight dip came from the newly recovered modes (85.71% on Place Shoe, 40.00% on Rotate QR Code), which were still harder to execute reliably. Thus, general capability was not degraded; rather, it reflects a trade-off from maintaining challenging alternative modes that Vanilla simply discarded.

Ablating when Hungarian matching should start (warmup duration) showed that applying it from epoch 0 lowered coverage by 5.13 points, while waiting too long (epoch 100) allowed mode collapse to set in. The authors established a unified, tuning-free rule: begin matching at the first checkpoint where the task metric reaches 60% and all modalities are still present in rollouts.

captions.F3: Overview of the five simulation tasks evaluated. From left: Push-T (2 modes), Stack Blocks (2 modes), Place Bread (2 modes), Place Shoe (4 modes), and Rotate QR Code (4 modes), all featuring symmetric action choices.
captions.F4: Real-world tasks on the Unitree G1 humanoid. Left: placing a banana onto a plate; Right: tossing an empty can into a bin. Both can be completed with either arm. Vanilla collapsed to using only one arm, while the proposed method preserved both arms in a 1:1 ratio.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Directions
sections.summary: This work identified diffusion path crossing in low-dimensional action spaces as the root cause of mode collapse, solving it with a simple noise assignment add-on during training. Improving execution reliability on newly recovered modalities remains an avenue for future work.
sections.details:
This study highlighted the mode collapse phenomenon where Diffusion Policy collapses to a single action mode even on balanced demonstrations, attributing it to path crossing and averaged denoising caused by independent action-noise pairing. Immiscible Diffusion Policy addresses this as a practical, label-free add-on that requires no changes to network architecture or inference, delivering strong multimodal preservation across simulation and real hardware.

As a limitation, when modalities completely abandoned by Vanilla are brought back, their execution success rates tend to be somewhat lower than the dominant modes. Ensuring equally high-quality control across all recovered action modalities remains an important direction for future research.

takeaways: Diffusion Policy has an inherent vulnerability to collapsing into a single action mode even on balanced and symmetric datasets due to diffusion path crossings during training.
Minimizing Euclidean distance between action chunks and noise samples via Hungarian matching within each mini-batch structures the noise space by modality and preserves diversity.
No modifications to model architectures, inference samplers, or loss functions are needed; it can be plugged into existing codebases simply by sorting noise during training.
Rather than matching from epoch 0, introducing noise assignment after basic task competencies emerge (around 60% task performance) provides optimal stability.
limitations: When difficult non-dominant modalities abandoned by Vanilla are recovered, their task success rates can be lower than those of the dominant modalities.
Because Hungarian matching is solved within batches, extremely small batch sizes might not provide sufficient structure to organize the noise space effectively.
